claim: The RLM paper proposes a general inference paradigm in which long prompts become part of an external environment that the model examines and recursively queries.
quote: We propose Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment and allows the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt.

claim: An independent reproduction found that applying deeper recursion (depth=2) or using RLMs on simple retrieval tasks degrades performance and inflates execution time and token costs.
quote: applying deeper recursion (depth=2) or using RLMs on simple retrieval tasks paradoxically degrades performance and exponentially inflates execution time (e.g., from 3.6s to 344.5s) and token costs.

claim: RLM-Extended, a systems-oriented extension of RLMs, adds local LLM backend support through an Ollama-based interface.
quote: local LLM backend support through an Ollama-based interface

claim: The CLM paper treats the context as a file that the model may update without restriction.
quote: We implement this by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to this file.

claim: The CLM authors report that, on the terminal-coding benchmark TerminalBench 2.1, CLM matches the strongest baseline's accuracy with 29.5% fewer FLOPs.
quote: while matching the strongest baseline's accuracy on the terminal-coding benchmark TerminalBench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) with 29.5% fewer FLOPs.

claim: The CLM authors also report that Suffix Cache Reuse lowers server-side compute relative to standard SGLang serving.
quote: Finally, we co-design Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving, further reducing server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.

claim: RLM is among the baselines in the CLM comparison, which used a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone.
quote: We compare CLMs against MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2026), Self-Compact (Li et al., 2026b), ACM (Li et al., 2026c), and recursive language models (RLM) (Zhang et al., 2025a) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone (Merrill et al., 2026).
locator: sec. Coding and Deep Research Tasks, para 23

claim: Serving-side work shows why in-place edits are a cache problem: Leyline states that production agentic harnesses fall back to re-prefill on every edit.
quote: Production agentic harnesses fall back to re-prefill on every edit, paying full prefix-recomputation cost

claim: Leyline reports that its splice kernel raises replay cache hits and cuts latency.
quote: The splice kernel lifts replay cache-hit by +11.2 pp and cuts latency by up to 241 ms.

claim: SMem, an architecture in which deletion is an exact update, reports that deletion beats suffix recomputation by 8.5× at 512 blocks and 452× at 4096 blocks.
quote: deletion beats suffix recomputation by 8.5$\times$ at 512 blocks and 452$\times$ at 4096 blocks

claim: Non-prefix reuse in general risks quality loss, as CacheTune's authors state.
quote: directly reusing KV Cache in non-prefix settings breaks the cross-chunk global attention relationships and causes significant degradation in generation quality.

claim: Other context-management work on coding agents gives token-level evidence. Focus reports a token reduction with identical accuracy on a very small sample.
quote: Focus achieves 22.7% token reduction (14.9M ->11.5M tokens) while maintaining identical accuracy (3/5 = 60% for both agents).

claim: Scroll reports token counts rather than latency or dollar cost.
quote: We report token counts rather than latency or dollar cost, as both depend on serving configuration.
